Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Selfee: Self-supervised Features Extraction of animal behaviors" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and K VijayRaghavan as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Mason Klein (Reviewer #1); Primoz Ravbar (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

The Reviewers agree that the paper presents a really exciting method that could have broad impact on researchers studying quantitative animal behavior. However there are some unresolved issues for establishing the credibility of the method that we would like you to address.

Essential revisions:

1) Chose one or two strong and clean datasets and take them all the way through the analysis pipeline (selfee->anomaly score->AR-HMM->DTW) instead of using different experiments for explaining different points. We suggest removing IR76b data from the story unless the experiment can be somehow justified.

2) Also show Selfee's results on a simpler data set (with Drosophila or some other animal) with single-animal video.

3) Explain the rationale behind the choice of parameters for "Selfee". Please explain why Selfee performs so poorly without the CLD component. Would a simpler architecture, with the addition of CLD, achieve similar performance as the Selfee?

4) Explore the behaviors found in different parts of the t-SNE maps and evaluate the effect of the irrelevant features on their distributions. The t-SNE maps display several clusters representing the same behaviors (Figure 2D) which suggests strong overfitting (weak generalization). The authors should at least show some examples taken from different clusters. This would illustrate why Selfee is separating behaviors that humans perceive as a single category.

5) Provide a formal comparison with one of the pre-existing methods that would in theory work on the same videos (e.g. JAABA) (Posted 6th Apr 2022).

6) Provide a supplementary table showing full genotype of all experimental animals.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall I like the paper! I will try to give as many specific, detailed comments as possible in this section.

First, to clarify some of the items I listed under "weaknesses" in the public review:

(1) Since the paper feels mainly like a Selfee methods paper, I think spending more time describing what exactly Selfee is and how it works would be appropriate. I would recommend putting an expanded version of the Methods section paragraph (lines 925-933) in the main body of the paper, briefly explaining the techniques and existing software as you go through each step. It would give a reader with little machine learning experience a better understanding of the process.

(2) Efficiency was talked about in the introduction and occasionally brought up when highlighting that Selfee doesn't need large computational/processing power to operate, but I didn't come away with a sense of how much Selfee improves on other approaches in this regard. It would be helpful to be more specific.

(3) The comparisons with DeepLabCut make sense -- if it would be straightforward to compare to other software, that might help highlight unique aspects of Selfee a bit more effectively.

(4) I don't usually recommend new experiments when I review papers, but perhaps showing Selfee's results on a simpler data set (with Drosophila or some other animal), say with single-animal video, before showing the courtship-type results, could ease a reader into the process more effectively.

(5) It would also be great, if possible, to include a small section that could operate like a guide for a novice user to try Selfee on their own data.

A few general comments:

(1) I am not a machine learning expert myself, so I hope another reviewer could evaluate Selfee's uniqueness compared to other methods, as I am taking that at face value in my review. In particular, (line 17-19), is this true that unsupervised analysis has not been used this way before?

(2) A fair amount of grammar/word usage errors, not really a problem and I assume copy editors will address? (e.g. Fast --> Quickly or Rapidly on line 15).

(3) I generally like the figures, but found Figure 2 and Figure 3 pretty difficult to read at that size. Rearranging the panels and/or using larger fonts would help readability considerably.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This work is very relevant but has some serious unresolved issues before warranting further consideration. The overall format of the paper will also have to be massively restructured to make it palatable for a wide, life-science research audience.

Major points of concern that need to be addressed:

1) In the way it is presented, the rationale behind choice of several of the parameters for "Selfee" are unclear to me. E.g.

a. Why do the live frames consist of 3 tandem frames? Is 3 somehow a special number that is easy to compute or represent as an RGB image? Why not 4 with CMYK or a higher number with a distinct colormap as is commonly done for representing depth coding.

b. The choice of AR-HMM and DTW as post-processing steps after the Selfee analysis is also a bit unclear to me. Especially because the authors do not discuss any alternatives and moreover, they don't even show great promise in the examples later in the manuscript.

2) The authors have surprisingly failed to acknowledge and cite the state of the field that directly translates to their novelty claims (Lines 56-59: "There are no pose estimation paradigms that are designed to handle multi-animal contexts"). Both multi-animal DLC (Lauer et al., 2021) and SLEAP (Perreira et al., 2020) were explicitly designed for this purpose. Not to mention a plethora tools for multi-animal behavioral classification, especially during social interactions that provide pretty much all the extracted information obtained using Selfee in this manuscript. Listing a few Drosophila specific tools:

a. JAABA (Kaabra et al., Nat Methods, 2013)

b. Matebook (Ribeiro et al., Cell 2018)

c. Flytracker (Hoopfer et al., eLife 2015)

3) The authors must provide a sup table showing full genotype of all experimental animals. Wherever possible test and controls should be in the same genetic background (this is especially true for loss of function experiments where vision and locomotion is an integral part of the behavior, like the ones done in this manuscript). Legends for videos should also be provided.

4) Figure 2 demonstrates how good Selfee is at extracting information. To do this, authors have to either look at how data clusters with respect to human annotated labels on a t-sne map or use a k-nn classification step to classify the data. Honestly, the t-sne maps in Figure 2D don't look that promising. K-nn classification looks better with around 70% F1 score. But at this point there should be a formal comparison with one of the pre-exisiting methods that would in theory work on the same videos. I suggest JAABA (or Flytracker+JAABA) since similar labels have been previously extracted using this toolkit. Same holds true for mouse data (2G-I) and especially more important because the F1 scores here are a bit low. Also panels 2F and 2I likely represent cherry picked cases where results are much better than what the scores indicate and hence are not really informative.

5) The rationale for definition of "anomaly score" (Figure 3, lines 230-249) is again poorly defended in the text. Could authors clearly define what "meta-representations of frames" means. Also, why restrict k=1 for IES? How is the +-50 frame window chosen for IAS score. Are these empirically derived values after some trial and error, or based on some priors. Since the anomaly score is quite central to the overall utility of this tool, it needs to be proposed in a much more credible way.

6) The unusual subset of neurotransmitter mutants/silenced lines used in Figure 3 data makes one wonder if the provided data is a cherry-picked subset of the full data to make the story easier. I would really appreciate if all data were shown clearly and rationally. The authors really need to establish credibility for persuading the reader to use their method.

7) Trh mutant phenotype is interesting but interpretations of secondary assays warrant some more thought. Trh neurons directly innervate Drosophila legs (Howard et al., 2019, Curr Biol.) and impact locomotion. Making a claim about social repulsion is a bit too ambitious without further segregating impact on other behaviors like walking that could impact the phenotype observed by the authors.

8) Given that the utility of AR-HMM rests on IR76b experiments which seem to be based on a false premise, it would be best if authors repeat this with one of the myriad of receptors shown to be involved in courtship. Or rather just do AR-HMM on one of the previous datasets.

9) DTW is a cool method but using increased copulation latency of blind flies to show its usability is a bit of a short-sell. It does not in any way increase the credibility of this method and I would rather suggest using DTW to look at longer scale dynamics in previous experiments (e.g. Figure 3 data), provided these are done in the correct genetic background).

Recommendation for improvement: The point of this paper is the method and not the biological findings. But the method loses credibility because there are serious problems with the way the experiments are performed and data is presented. I would recommend the authors chose one strong and clean dataset and take it all the way through their analysis pipeline (selfee->anomaly score->AR-HMM->DTW) instead of using different experiments for explaining different points. Even if the results are less interesting, if the rationale is clear and all data is shown properly this will encourage other people to try out this tool.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The figures are in a good shape, except where specifically mentioned (and assuming that the final published figures will have better resolution).

Major concerns (2):

1) Reference [9] is critically important for the understanding of how the CLD is implemented in this architecture, however, I find it difficult to access the reference. The authors should provide for an alternative. Adding more visualization of how the CLD is implemented, in Figure 2, would be helpful. The authors should compare the classification performance of Selfee with and without the CLD (for fly courtship behavior in Figure 2). This way the reader could understand the weight of the CLD in the overall architecture. Next, the authors should discuss alternative architectures with CLD and show why the SimSiam has been chosen.

2) How much of the performance of the classification (and possibly other utilities) is lost to strict end-to-end processing? The authors should show the effects of the following pre-processing steps on the t-SNE maps, the confusion matrices, and the F1 scores: a) use the raw frames instead of live-frames; b) perform simple background subtraction; c) create narrow areas of interest around the animals in each frame. Authors can add other steps such as segmentation. The prediction would be that the classification performance will improve greatly, the t-SNE maps should have fewer yet more distinct clusters, and rare behaviors should be classified better than, for example, in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 F.

Although the F1 score was only 49.6%, it still captured the major differences between similar behaviors, such as allogrooming and social nose contact (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

results.result: Selfee is a self-supervised CNN that processes video frames end-to-end by stacking three consecutive frames into 'live-frames' and training a SimSiam-style network with data augmentation to extract discriminative, comprehensive representations invariant to shooting conditions, translation, and rotation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21-23, C26-28, C33-34, C36-37 collectively describe the Selfee architecture and training approach with clear methodological details, figures, and experimental validation. The live-frame construction, network architecture (ResNet-50 backbone with MLP projector), and training strategy are well-documented with supporting figures (Figure 1A-B, Figure 2).

results.result: Selfee extracts features that align with human perception of fly courtship behaviors, achieving 72.4% F1 score in k-NN classification and capturing fine-grained features like wing angles and spatial positioning that separate behavioral subtypes on t-SNE visualization.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C38-44 are supported by Figure 3A-C showing t-SNE clustering of human-annotated behaviors, quantitative classification metrics (72.4% F1 score comparable to human inter-rater agreement of ~70%), and supplementary figures demonstrating feature separation by wing angle and distance. The comparison to human performance (C44) provides appropriate context.

results.result: Selfee features are comparably discriminative to animal-tracking derived features (FlyTracker, JAABA) while requiring no manual key point definition or feature engineering, achieving best performance by Pearson's correlation (0.774) and F1 score (0.629) in comparative evaluation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-48, C98 are supported by Table 1 showing quantitative comparisons across multiple feature types and evaluation metrics. The ablation demonstrates that pure distance-based features can be discriminative but lack abstraction (C47), while Selfee balances discrimination with interpretability without requiring careful feature engineering.

results.result: Selfee generalizes to mice mating behaviors, achieving 67.4% F1 score with LightGBM classifier when incorporating temporal features, with live-frames proving more discriminative than single frames for highly dynamic behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-50, C55 are supported by Figure 3D-F showing t-SNE separation of five behavior types and quantitative classification results. Table 3 provides ablation evidence that live-frames outperform single frames for mice behaviors. The need for temporal aggregation (81-frame windows) and ensemble methods suggests the task is challenging but the approach is effective.

results.result: Architectural modifications including group discriminators (CLD loss) and Turbo augmentation significantly improve Selfee performance, preventing mode collapse and enhancing feature discrimination as demonstrated by ablation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-54 are supported by ablation studies in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Tables 2-3. The CLD loss prevents catastrophic mode collapse (collapse level near 1.0 without it vs. <0.01 with it), and Turbo augmentation improves F1 scores. The mechanistic explanation for CLD addressing long-tail effects and mode collapse is reasonable given the imbalanced nature of behavioral data.

results.result: Selfee enables frame-level anomaly detection that identifies ultra-fast (<0.25s) behaviors in CCHa2-R-RB>Kir2.1 flies that are difficult for human observers to detect, using cosine distance with intra-group score correction to reduce false positives.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C56-62 are supported by Figure 4A-D showing the anomaly detection methodology and results. The identification of brief tussle behavior in CCHa2-R-RB>Kir2.1 flies (C59-61) is documented with temporal dynamics (Figure 4D) showing sub-second duration. The IAS correction (C58) addresses a methodological challenge with false positives, though the need for this correction suggests the method requires careful tuning.

results.result: Selfee discovered that Trh knockout flies exhibit reduced social distance and defensive behavior, validating the anomaly detection with follow-up behavioral assays showing significantly lower kicking rates and shorter inter-fly distances, representing a novel behavioral phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-71 are supported by Figure 4B, E-J showing anomaly detection results and validation experiments. The statistical significance of kicking behavior (p=0.0034, C68) and social distances (C69) provides strong validation. However, the novelty claim (C67) relies on authors' knowledge and may require more thorough literature review. The biological interpretation connecting serotonin to social distance is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: AR-HMM analysis of Selfee features successfully distinguishes control from CIS-treated mice in open field tests, identifying two behavioral modules with significantly different usage patterns related to wall proximity, consistent with previous observations of anxiety-like behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30-31, C72-78 are supported by Figure 5A-D showing AR-HMM methodology and results. The statistical significance of module usage differences (p=0.00065 and p=0.015 with correction, C75) and consistency with prior work (Ramirez et al., 2015, C76, C78) strengthen the findings. The interpretation linking modules to spatial behavior is validated by tracking data (C77).

results.result: DTW analysis of Selfee features captures long-term behavioral dynamics, revealing delayed courtship in NorpA mutant flies with prolonged latency, demonstrating the method can detect temporal differences beyond single-frame postures.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C79-84 are supported by Figure 5E-G showing DTW methodology and results. The prolonged courtship latency in NorpA mutants (p=0.0495, C81) is consistent with prior findings (Markow and Manning, 1980), and the DTW curve below diagonal (C82) correctly indicates delay. The application of DTW to image-derived features rather than traditional numerical measures is novel.

results.result: The complete Selfee pipeline (preprocessing, feature extraction, AR-HMM, DTW, anomaly detection) can evaluate animal behaviors in a purely unsupervised manner without human-defined behaviors or key points, as demonstrated on mice OFT data where results from Selfee embeddings strongly match position-based analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-91 are supported by Figure 6 showing the complete pipeline demonstration. The consistency between Selfee embeddings and position-based DTW (C89, Figure 6C) validates the approach. However, the very low anomaly rate (12 frames, <0.01%, C85) classified as false positives (C86) suggests limited sensitivity for this particular comparison, though this doesn't invalidate the overall pipeline.

results.result: Selfee achieves zero-shot domain transfer, successfully applying models trained on mice mating behavior to single-animal OFT and achieving 49.6% F1 score on rat social behaviors without retraining, demonstrating cross-species and cross-paradigm generalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-113 are supported by experimental results showing successful application to OFT (C110-111) and rat behaviors (C112, Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The 49.6% F1 score for rats is modest but demonstrates meaningful transfer learning. This is a significant practical advantage, though the performance degradation suggests domain-specific training remains beneficial for optimal results.

results.result: Selfee can be trained on a single RTX 3090 GPU in 8 hours with batch size 256 and accepts standard 2D grayscale video, making it accessible to biology laboratories without specialized hardware like depth cameras or multi-view arrays.
results.evaluation: Claims C108, C120-122 provide specific quantitative details about computational requirements that are verifiable from the methods section. The 8-hour training time and 800 fps inference speed represent significant practical advantages over methods requiring 8+ GPUs or TPUs (C107). The accessibility claim (C122) is a reasonable inference from these specifications.

results.result: Selfee complements pose estimation methods by handling closely interacting animals where DeepLabCut, FlyTracker, and SLEAP show tracking errors, though Selfee features are less explainable than key points and benefit from animal tracking for interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C99-106 are supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing tracking failures during close interactions for all three pose estimation methods tested. The complementary nature is well-argued: Selfee handles occlusions (C104) but lacks explainability (C105). The acknowledgment of limitations (C105) and potential for integration (C106) demonstrates balanced assessment.

results.result: Selfee has limitations including limited motion capture from 3-frame live-frames, vulnerability to background textures requiring preprocessing in some cases, and potential mode-split from batch-level discrimination without negative samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-117 honestly acknowledge limitations with supporting evidence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for texture effects, C116). These are reasonable limitations given the architectural choices. The mode-split issue (C117) is a known challenge in self-supervised learning without negative samples, though the CLD loss partially addresses this.

results.result: Prior to this work, no end-to-end unsupervised neural network extracted comprehensive features directly from social behavior video frames, and pose estimation methods had not been demonstrated on multiple same-colored animals with intensive interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C13 make assertions about gaps in the literature based on authors' knowledge. While the authors demonstrate their method addresses these gaps, comprehensive verification of these negative claims would require exhaustive literature review. The claims are plausible given the cited limitations of existing methods, but cannot be definitively verified from the manuscript alone.

results.result: Self-supervised learning methods extract features by comparing augmented images, avoiding human bias, achieving invariance to size/orientation/illumination without preprocessing, and producing inherently discriminative features even without negative samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-20 accurately describe properties of self-supervised learning supported by multiple citations (Caron et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Grill et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018). These are well-established principles in the field. However, the claim of 'completely avoiding human biases' (C17) is somewhat overstated, as architectural choices and augmentation strategies still involve human decisions.

results.result: Siamese CNNs with cosine similarity provide a rational framework for end-to-end feature extraction that can be flexibly combined with various downstream analyses including t-SNE, k-NN, AR-HMM, and DTW.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-96 are supported by citations (C92) and demonstrated through multiple successful applications in the results. The versatility claim (C95-96) is validated by the diverse downstream analyses presented. The assertions about cosine similarity (C93) and end-to-end training (C94) are standard properties of these architectures.

results.result: Future improvements could include advanced self-supervised methods like DINO with visual transformers to separate objects from background, extract more explainable representations, and achieve robustness against distractive textures.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-119 are speculative suggestions for future work supported by citations (Caron et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2021). While these are reasonable directions based on recent advances in computer vision, they represent untested hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. The claims are appropriately framed as future possibilities rather than current achievements.

results.result: Selfee was validated on three model species (flies, mice, rats) with results consistent with manual annotations, animal tracking methods, and biological experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-25 are supported by extensive experimental validation throughout the results section including comparisons to human annotations (Figure 3), animal tracking (Table 1), and biological validation experiments (Figure 4G-J). The multi-species validation strengthens generalizability claims.
